summary:
Ryazan Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia. The sources contain no oblast-specific or Central Federal District-specific findings, so the region is assessed at the national score rather than on local evidence.

The baseline recorded in the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) is that same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections exist. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law banning gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed.

The 'gay propaganda' statute carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to four years in prison, and the expanded version of the law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. The Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation carries two to six years' imprisonment for participating and six to ten for organising.

Foreign nationals who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation. Official national government warnings state this explicitly to LGBT travellers, and the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, carrying warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Enforcement is documented at volume: between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, and courts had issued 101 extremism convictions tied to the 2023 designation as of 30 June 2025.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is escalating in both volume and severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two preceding years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was recorded by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Detention itself carries lethal risk. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man held on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility, and Human Rights Watch recorded one person dying by suicide in pretrial detention between January 2024 and June 2025.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025, with a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

Protection machinery runs in the opposite direction: the UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition and no access to gender-affirming care, both prohibited by the 2023 law; same-sex marriage is unavailable and no specific anti-discrimination protections exist.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) recorded 101 convictions for extremism tied to the International LGBT Movement designation. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, courts sentenced two to prison, and 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. Participation in the designated movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it six to ten; propaganda offences carry administrative fines escalating to four years on repetition.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Ryazan Oblast-specific or Central Federal District-specific findings appear in any source; the region's national-score assessment rests entirely on the national baseline in the UK Home Office note, and no local enforcement record for this oblast was located.

The sources disagree on the upper penalty attached to extremist-designation participation: the UK Home Office note gives two to six years for participating and six to ten for organising, while the Human Rights Watch item refers to participants facing up to 12 years in prison. The basis for the higher figure is unresolved.

The UK Home Office note is cited in two versions across the inventory — June 2025 with the assessment updated 11 June 2025, and a page updated 12 August 2026. Which version governs the current baseline is unresolved.

The conversion-therapy case documented by BBC Russian occurred in 2021 near Novosibirsk, outside this oblast; it evidences a national pattern of coercive practice rather than a local one, and no comparable case in Ryazan Oblast is sourced.
